The March of Freedom.
For at least Bix or seven vears, a
powerful party in Brazil has been struggling
for the emancipation of the slaves in that
great empire. At last a bill abolishing
the institution has passed both houses
of the legislative body. It is a very
complicated affair, and has many
positive faults; but the passage at all of
such a measure is a great stride in the
progress of Freedom, which all friends
of humanity shounld be heartily
thankful for. No longer ago than 1849,
Brazil was importing more than fifty
thousand slaves a year. In 1850 she
declared the trade to be piracy, and since then
her men-of-war have shown
considerable zeal and industry in overhauling
slavers. When we remember that the
domain of Brazil is equal to the eutire
territory of the United States, with vast

natural resources, and that she already
has a population of at least thirteen
millions - greater than the population
of our slave-holding States before the
war - the importance of her
emancipation may be appreciated. The bill met
the violent opposition of most of "the
slave-owners, and was even fought by
some of the radical abolitionists, on the
ground that it put too many restrictions
upon the freedmen; but that it should
pass at all, is a hopeful sign for still
better days that must be coming speedily;
and another, perhaps a stronger one,
may be found in the fact that the slaves
themselves have already breathed enough
of the air of freedom to be clamorous
for complete liberty as their right, and
in one province they recently raised a
gerious insurrection,

Work for Women.
It will be remembered that in the
remarkable discourse of Bishop Doane, at
the consecration of Bishop Niles in this
city, a year ago, one noticeable point
was a plea for the establishment of
sisterhoods in which pious women could
find a home and devote themselves to
charitable work under the protection and
direction of the church. This idea seems
to be growing in the Episcopal church,
at least in that portion of it having
highchurch or ritualistic tendencies. The
General Convention, now in session at
Baltimore, has under consideration a
resolution recommending the
establishment of such a sisterhood, for the
training of women to be nurses, teachers,
and domestic missionaries, ''such
women not to be bound by irrevocable
vows, and to be able to return to the
house where they were trained, when
disabled, with the assurance of a
comfortable support through life." That the

idea will be put into practice ere lon"g, is
quite probable; and that, looked at from
a worldly business point of view, it will
strengthen the Episcopal church, seems
equally certain. The plan will furnish
a partial solution to the 'surplus
women" problem; and one of the causes
which Macaulay sets' forth in his fine
analysis of the power of the Roman
church, will be found, we presume,
nearly or quite as active in the Protestant.

farming. A few days ago the senior class
went in a body to the Sagadahoc county
fair. intent on investigating the greatest
pumpkinian achievements and the latest
thingin superphosphates. As they could
not be in two places at once, without
violating a well established law of nature,
the professors necessarily found their
class-rooms empty, whose echoss had
rest from conic sections and Compte's
philosophy. But the faculty, ungrateful
for the rare relief, and unappreciative of
the agricultural instinct, have suspended
the entire class.

Gorrespondence of the Independent Statesman,
FROM NEW YORK,
Effects of the Chicago Fire - Decline in Stocks -
The Insurance Business - History of the Great
Companies - The Failures and
Successes - Extraordinary Precautions - On Shipboard - Fire-Proof
Buildings - &e.
New York, Oct. 24, 1871.
The extraordinary effect of a great
public calamity, like the Chicago fire,
upon general values, is one of its most
striking aspects. For instance, the
depression in stocks, which was
immediately felt in Wall street, was almost
equal to the entire damage of the
conflagration. A part of this might have been
referable to the destruction of railway
depots and similar damage at that
locality ; but this loss is trifling in
comparison with the fall in prices. The Lake
Shore road lost its depot and was
damaged to the extent of a half million. Two
years ago the same amount was sunk by
the failure of its agency in this city, but

that did not effect the stock in the least.
The capital is fifty millions, which is too
large an interest to be impaired by any
such trifling loss. The depreciation of
Lake Shore stock since the fire, however,
is equal to five millions. The New York
Central lost nothing by the fire, and yet
the shrinkage in its value is about nine
millions. An equal loss may be figured
on a score of important railways and
similar institutions. and hence the
depreciation in values cannot be much less
than $200,000,000. This is producing a
severe calamity among a vast number,
and shows how widely the effects of
such a catastrophe may spread.

A vastly greater loss has overcome the
insurance companies, which suffer to the
extent of $57,000,000. I have been
acquainted with the inception of many of
these institutions, some of which have
run a very successful career, until
suddenly brought to ruin. The insurance
business had a great expaunsion in this
city in 1850, when a large number 'of
new companies was formed. Among
these were the Merchants', the Lorillard,
the Excelsior, the Commonwealth, the
Ivving, the Niagara, and others. The
history of these institutions affords a
very interesting view of the risks of
insuranceand the importance of good
management. Like the children in a large
family, some grow vigorously, some live
in a pining and dwarfed condition, and
some die early. The Commonwealth was
ruined by bad management, and stopped
business a year ago. Its stockholders
realized sixty per cent., which is more

than they would have got had the
company continued up to the Chicago fire.
This company ha(? paid good dividends
for eighteen years, and the writer held
a policy in it for a large part of that time.
The Astor paid from eight to twelve per
cent. annually, and would have
continued thus had it not injudiciously taken
risks in Chicago to an amount larger
than its capital. The Lorillard paid from
twelve to sixteen per cent., and was
considered a prosperous institution until the
Chicago fire, in which, like the Astor, it
had too heavy a risk. The same may be
said of the Irving and the Excelsior.

Oun the other hand, the Niagara paid
twenty per cent. for ten years, and since
then has paid ten per cent., and although
it loses heavily in Chicago, it is still a
valuable stock. The Merchants' is the
best off of all these new companies. It
commenced with a capital of $200,000,
and has paid about twenty per cent. per
annum for the past twenty years. Its
capital and vesources now amount to
about $430,000, and its losses at Chicago
are only &15,000, while the Lorillard
sank over $300,000 there. The great
success of the Merchants' is beyond my
penetration. Its officers are not
distinguished above other business men, and
it took risks upon the same laws and
calculations on which other men operate.

Its stock must have been under the
influence of what people generally call
''good luck," and it has proved a very
handsome investment.
The recent advance in the rates of
insurance will make the business very
profitable, and on this account the stocks
of the surviving companies have
advanced. Escape from the Chicago fire is
now a great card of advertising, and
you may see the frequent announcement
placarded, '" This office had nothing with
Chicago." One of the best of the old
companies is the Bowery, whose stock is
worth 150. Another is the Equitable,
which has sold since the Chicago fire .at
167. They pay twenty per cent. per
annum, and have o large surplus. The
folly of taking extensive risks in Chicago
is now apparent. It was a wooden city,
where a firc would always be very
dangerous, and in a dry season must be
peculiarly so. New York suffers severely

at times, even with brick and stone.
'What, then, must be the risk in a city
vghle?re wood is the chief building
materia
ADDITIONAL PRECAUTION.
The insurance business will be
assisted,by the fact that a much greater degree
of ?reca.ution will begenerally exercised.
Half of our fires are occasioned by the
most culsable carelessness, and this will
be abated by the fearful lesson which we
have just received. The writer has for
several years kept a cask of water on
each floor of his dwelling, with pails,
ready to meet the danger of fire. The
water is charged with salt, to keep it
from becoming offensive, and there it
stands year after vear. This precaution
may have appeared excessive to some;
but how often a fire which a few pails of
water might have extinguished has
resulted in prodigious destruction. My

insurance is now worthless, and 1 must,
for a while at least, take my own risk,
Amongother acts of carelessness which
have resulted disastrously, the most
remarkable was that of an employe in
Harper's book establishment. He had
Justlighted a match, which, when used,
he should have blown out, or
extinguished with his foot. Instead of doing
this, he threw it, all ablaze, into an open
taqk containing spirits of tm'pentf:\e.
Within two hours the whole
establishment was in rains, with a loss of $250,-
000, This occurred in 1854, and many
similar cases have happened since. It is
instructing at such times as these, to
recall the precautions used in our navy.

One of the chief of these is the rule that
when the magazine is to be opened every

fire aboard the vessel must first be
extinguished. The firein Portland, in 1864,
was oczasioned by a boy who threw a
lighted Chinese fire-cracker intoa barrel
of shavings. I might extend these
illustrations with great propriety. How
many houses have been fired by hot
wood-ashes placed in barrels! Indeed,
one of the worst fires that ever occurred
in Troy was occasioned in this way, and
probably many more will arise from the
same kind of carelessness. Ourmethod
of illumination is to a large degree
dangerous. (s in this city is enormously
expensive, and hence most of the
population use kerosene oil. Before this
article was discovered, a very combustible
and dangerous compound called "
burning-fluid" was in use, by which many
fires were occasioned. Whale-oil and
candles are now expensive, and hence
kerosene is in common use; but it is a

question whether it is not the dearest,
after all.
WHO DO NOT INSURE.
Large landed proprietors in this city
take their own risk of fire, for the
simple reason that this is the cheapest
method, William B. Astor ownssix hundred
houses, the insurance on which would
cost $30,000 a year. It is not probable
that the fire risk costs him one quarter
of that amount. James Lenox, Peter
Goelet,and the Hendricks, the Lorillards,
and other real-estate men, are equally
profited by being their own
underwriters. As a rule, it is said that if a
business will not pay enough to afford
insurance, it will not pay to follow it; hence
most men insure, for at least a part of
their risk. Some persons, however, go
through life without iusurance and
without loss. The writer has seen
remarkable vagaries of fire risks. The very best

buildings in this city have been burned,
while the poorest have escaped. The
very poverty of their inmates has often
saved themn from one of the greatest
sources of danger - the flues of furnaces.
A great many tires have occurred from
this cause; but no poor man could think
of heating his apartments in this manner.
The tenement-houses, whichcontain large
numnbers of families, instead of being the
most dangerous, seldom take fire,
because there are so many to watch the
premises. Our large establishments
generdlly have a fire apparatus of their own.

The Fifth Avenue Hotel has an enormous
reservoir, and the water is propelled by
the engine which does the general work
of the house. By attaching a hose and
turning on the steam, a powerful stream
can be thrown to theroof. The servants
form a suitable fire brigade, and once a
week they are drilled in this service.
More than five hundred of these
exercises have taken place, after theé fashion
of a sham fight, and should a fire ever
happen there, it will be met by skill and
determination. R e
I have often noticed in the
establishment of the Evening Post the printed
fire-regulations, which are posted on
every floor. Full directions are here
given how to turn on the steam so that
the hose can at any time be made
available, and the locality of the axes and

other implements is given,
Such precautions are common in other
large establishments. On some of the
British steamers the fire-alarm is
purposely given once during every voyage,
and the passengers are at first thrown
into a panic; but they are soon relieved
when they see the perfection with which
the arrangements are carried out
forbattling with the dreadful element.

FIRE-PROOF BUILDINGS.
A great deal has been said, in a
boastful way, about our fire-proof buildings;
but the lesson of Chicago leads us to
doubt their security, If these buildings
be not burned, they may be converted
into vastovens,and their
contentsthusdestroyed with intense heat. But most of
our so-called fire-proof buildings could
be burned, or at least destroyed, by a
great fire. It is possible that the
Treasury might escape. It is of solid stone,
with small windows protected with iron,
and has a stone roof. The Custom House,
being of granite, is fire-proof also, unless
its metal roof should be penetrated by a
hostile flame. Aside from these and the
new Court House, there is hardly a
structure in the city that would not,
under the same circumstances, share the
fate of the best buildings in Chicago. It
is only at such times that the power of

fire is demonstrated. Then it is seen
that the incombustible burns without
difficulty. As the man remarked of the
fire-proof Chicago post-office, that ¢it
seemed to burn very well," so it may be
said of other boasted edifices. Diana's
tem({)le at Epbesus was no doubt
considered fire-proof until Erostratus
immortalized himself by burningit. Andif the
woman that was milking the cow at
Chicago on Sunday night, October Bth, when
the latter kicked over the lamp and
burncd the city, could be known, she would
have a better chance of immortality than
MARTEL.

THE INSURANCE QUESTION. An
examination into the condition of the
insurance companies which held risks on
Chicago property reveals the fact that
fifty-oneare virtually insolvent or
hopelessly embarrassed, and that two or three
more will probably be obliged to
suspend. All of the corporations are doing
their best, undoubtedly, being well
aware of the advantage *which will be
acquired hereafter by every company
having large risks in the burned city
weathering the gale. Of those reported
insolvent nearly one-half are in this
State, twelve in Chicago, twelve in New
England, five in Ohio, and one in
California. Itis understood that there are
other companies which will find it
difficult to avoid insolvency, but hope to
continue business, Yet, taking the
amount of capital represented in tge
assets of the companies, and that of the
loss of property in Chicago, it is
estimated that the return to the insured

will be considerably over fift per cent.
on 'their insurance. - New };rk

POSSESSED.
| BY FLORENCE .\I'LANDBI'RU.
~ During my youth I suffered from a
'naturally delicate constitution. I was
' pale, feeble, and sickly, but from no
'del cided disease. A dreamy, quiet cast
of temperament caused me to shrink
from the rough sports of my brothers:
the contact of strangers was equally
disagreeable, and I seldom strayed from
home. Indeed, I lived almost wholly
within myself; although by no means
devoid of natural affection; on the
contrary, my emotions were strong, and my
sympathy easily aroused. How it
hapened that I acquired a love of learning
})do not know, all the outward
circamstances by which I was surrounded
tending to foster anything rather than
intellectual habits; for our family, although
each member possessed a common
education, were strictly practical; but this
difference in my disposition cut. e off
from their pursuits, and I found my

chief enjoyment in the volumes of a
library to which I obtained access.
Perhaps it was the sedentary life I led,
the close confinement, and lack of
exercise, that brought on a violent .attack of
sickness when I was'in my nineteenth
'year, 80 that Ilay for several weeks
completely prostrated. During two or three
| gays my life hung as in'a balance, which
a breath might have turned and launched
me beyond the confines of time.
However, the disease succumbed to the
persevering attention of experienced nurses,
I arose from my weary bed and found
my physical health slowly improving,
but from that period I was subject at
irregular intervals to what the physician
ronounced temporary delirium, which
Fknow he used as a milder term for
insanity.

But it was not insanity. I never lost
control of my mind; but I lost control
of my body. Itobeyed a will that was
not my own. A mighty antagonistic
power seemed to creep over my brain,
which impelled my movements and held
my struggling soul in subjection. I
pregented the singular phenomenon of one
person governed by two separate and
distinet wills, for my mind was not
disordered, but only mastered by superior
strength. In this strange condition I
would see familiar objects magnified,
exaggerated,contorted, inan atmosphere
varying with all colors, at the same time
being perfectly consciousof theirreal
appearance. I would hear sounds sweet'
and musical grow into wails of
heartrending despair. I could recognize my
friends when they were present, but was
forced to regard them with the cold eye
of a stranger. I would commit acts that

no human agency could have compelled
me to do when my faculties were un- '
trammeled. I never submitted without
a struggle, and always felt conscious
that, it Icould but once resist this
seemingly-invincible power, if I could but
once disregard its promptings, I should
be free; but my soul was fettered.
The attacks were never of long
duration. They always left me utterly
exhausted, and it would sometimes require

a week to recruit my expended strength.
I could afterward recall every incident
with the most distinct minuteness, for
they were branded in characters of fire
on my memory. Vainly I asserted again
and again that it was not delirium, that
I was forced into subjection to some
mysterious power I could not withstand ;
my statements made no impression upon
the physician, who evidently considered
mine but a common case of one
suffering from attacks of temporary insanity,
and when I persisted in my statement,
he forbade any further reference to the
subject. However, I could not prevent
my mind from continually dwelling
upon it in secret. What was this so foreign,
80 antagonistic to myself, that mastered
my will, that controlled my actions,
that made me literally another being?

Why did I not shake off this influence
and be free? I felt perfectly conscious!
of possessing the power, but was not!
able to arouse it from a latent
condition.
As I have said before, I was naturally
of a studious digposition, and I now
turned my attention to metaphysics. I
read works, ancient and modern, on its
different branches; I studied medical
treatises on insanity, and, the more I
learned, the more thoroughly convinced
I became that I was not suffering from
mental aberratien. Constant brooding
over my disease greatly wore upon my
physical strength: travelling was
recommended, in hopes that change of climate
and scene might benefit my health. My
old aversion to strangers clung to me,
and, although possessed by a restlessness
to which I was wholly unaccustomed, I
persistently refused to leave home; no
arguments could gain my consent, so

that my friends were forced to give up
the project in despair.
One morning, when more than the
usual gloom oppressed my spirits, I
made an effort to arouse myself and
throw off the melancholy that was
setting upon me, which each day I felt to
'be growing more confirmed. I was
sittling by a window, which stood wide
'open, and, just outside, a caged canary
was singing and fluttering its feathers
in the spring sunshine. The little bird
was my particular property, and I
regarded it with an aflgction whichis
rare1y bestowed npon pets. With the
exception of young sister, a child about
four years of age, this was the only
living thing that I had taken any interest
in since my sickness. I had trained the
canary from the shell, and thelittle
creatare scemed to repay all my care, for

from no other member of the family
would it receive caresses. I was so much
afraid of its being accidentally injured
that I never allowed it to be freed from
the cage except in my presence. At my
call it would fly about me, resting on'my
head, shoulders, or hands, chirping ina
perfect ecstasy of enjoyment.

I arose and opened the door of its
prison, then, reseating myself, softly
whistled while it darted into the air, wheeled
once or twice, and descended upon my
hand. Stroking its spotless vellow
plumage, I regarded the little thing with a
degree of pleasure I had notexperienced
for several weeks. But sudden horror
'almost caused my heart to cease its
beatings, and the perspiration started from i
my forehead in great drops, for I feltny
fingers slowly closing over the delicate I
bird. Although I made anattempt great- |
er than the racking effort we sometimes l
exert in the nightmare, I had no power '
to restrain them. The canary fluttered |
in my clasp. I would have dropped it,
I would have shrieked for help, but my
museles, my voice, my body, obeyed me ;
not, and my fingers, like the steady

working of machinery, gradually tight- '
ened their relentless grasp. In my
agony the veins of my face protruded like
lines of cordage. I heard the frail bones
breaking beneath the cruel pressure,
then my involuntary grip suddenly
relaxed, and the bird fell upon my knee,
dead and mangled.
At the same moment 1 saw, through
the open door, my little sister playing
upon the grass-plat; and, almost before
I was aware of moving, or of any
volition, I found myself walking rapidly
toward her, while my fingers twitched
'with a convulsive, clatching movement.

Good Heavens! Talready saw her face
turn purple, and heard her gaspin§
breath smothered by gurgling blood.
With this terrible picture before my
mental vision, my brain felt as if it
would burst'its bounds in the desperate
but unavailing efforts 1 made to turn
back, to fly from the spot. But I could
not command myself. In that moment
lendured suffering more intense than
language can describe. Perhaps my
strange and wild appearance frightened
the child; for, in' place of holding out
her arms to me, her favorite brother,she
fled crying to the nurse, who did not
observe my approach, and carried her into
the house. Saved! unconsciously saved
- saved from a fate too terrible to
contemplate.

I sank insensible upon the ground,
and, when I recovered, found myself
surrounded by the family, each one apFlying some restorative, for I had been
n a long and death-like swoon. Slowly
but distinctly the recollections of the
events which had reduced me to this
condition E)resented themselves to my
memory with all their appalling horror,
nearly depriving me again of
consciousness.
1 did not refer'in any manner to the
subgect, which was also carefully
avoided by all others in my presence, for fear
that it might produce renewed
excitement, and my friends had no suspicion
of the circumstances that brought it
about. The bird was found deag upon
the floor, and the family imagined that it
had met with some accident. They were
evidently surén-ised, when the fact was
communicated to me, that I made no
remarks, for they had anticipated an

outburst of grief. Grief! I did not
suffer from grief; grief was
overpowered by the horror that racked my brain -
horror for the act I had committed, and
the more fearful one which had been so
mercifully prevented. I had committed?
No, it was not my mind or will which
had prompted my hand to do the deed,
I was innocent, even though my fingers
had drip})ed with the blood of a sister;
but the frightful thought filled me with
a terror that wrung my soul. Ipondered

continually upon it. When might not
this mysterious demon again assert its
evil control over me? Strange as it may
seem, I felt certain that it was some
foreign agency - l knew not what - that
'mastered my will, and not the result of
my own intellect in a disordered
condi'tion.
This overpowering dread of the future
- of "what might happen - which took
possession of me, drove me to the
decision of leaving hoire, as the best way of
avoiding danger to my friends.
Perhaps, too, if my physical health became
better, I might gain strength enough to
defy this infernal power; for, as I have
said before, 1 possessed a singular
cousciousness that, if I could once
successfully resistits promptings, my soul would
be liberated from thraldom. lannounced
my determination of making a journey..

without any explanation of my sudden
change, and it was greeted with delight
by my friends and relatives, who were
anxious to hasten my departure while
the humor was upon me; but they need
not have feared any change of purpose
on my part, for I was haunted ll))y this
terrible dread of the future, and I gladly
said favewell fora time to my home aund
birth-place. - oo

The incidents of travel and of new
scenes broke the monotony, and
dispelled to some degree the gloom that had
taken fast hold upon me. In a short
period I found myselfrapidly improving.
Every week bronght me an increase ot
strength, and I suffered less frequently
from those frightful attacks. Although
they occurred at longer intervals than
formerly, they seemed to fFrow more
severein character; theconflict was fiercer,
and my mind made a more desperate
effort to gain the supremacy. My whole
frame would be racked by the intense
struggle which I constantly' maintained,
though constantly vanquished.

The increasing delight 1 took in the
beauties of nature, the continued
exercise andexcitement, almostdrove despair
from me, and hopeonce more brightened
my countenance. I began to look
forward to the time when my health would
be entirely restored, and my body and
mind be in unison. Idid not hope
vainly, for the final conflict came, and with
it a strange termination of my long
sufferings.
I stood upon the side of an Eastern
mountain. Above my head vast rocks
rose insolemn grandeur, their summits
lost in canopied mists which, gray and
clinging, wrapped them in obscurity.

Below, agreat chasm rent themountain;
a yawning, bottomless gulf. When I
gazed, awed by the thought of its
myssterious depths, where no human eye
had seen, where no human foot had trod,
a ray of light struggled in and rested on
gaunt trees, on snake-like ferns, damp -
and cold, that clung to its slimy sides, .
and on one pale flower which nodded in
the chill draught that came up, a
palpable horror, from the blackness of dark--
ness. I tarned awa{. Near the western
horizon dead clouds were piled
oneabove another, and their heavy shadow
lay brown and dark upon the sullen
earth. No wind stirred the forests, or
rustled their motionless leaves, and the
awe of the unbroken silence fell with &
dread oppression, upon my heart.

Suddenly I was seized by an ungovern--
able desire to possess the flower - the
colorless flower that hung far down in
the death-damp of the chasm. A
freezing terror crept through my blood as 1
recognized this decree of a will I had
never been able to disobey. I felt
myself crawling closer to the verge of the
precipice ; nearer, vet nearer, until I sat
withinthe very jaw of the savage gulf.
My feet dangled in the air, and the
ground quivered beneath my weight.

The dead clouds heaved their
shroudlike forms, and wavered overhead. I
'heard the rush of subterranean
waterssounding a muffled requiem. The sickly
flower, with its long stem, writhed and:
twisted like a serpent stretching his folds
into the air, swayed slowly back and
forth, glaring at me like a lustreless eye.
In spite of all my efforts to assert my
own will, in spite of my clear conviction
that my life was in deadly peril, I could
not throw off the fascination that
enthralled me, and was about to yield
passively to the demoniac influence and let
myself fall from the precipice, when a
voice apparently above me, a voice that
was not the voice of the tempter, began
to utter the Lord's prayer.
Instinctively I took up the invocation, which badi
not passed my lips for years, and repeat--

ed it with the fervid energy of despair;.
not unmingled with hope. As it ended. .
a convulsive shudder shook my frame; L
drew back, or was drawn back - l could
hardly tell which - from the verge of the
precipice, and sank insensible upon the
ground.
How long my swoon lasted, I cannot
say. When I returned to consciousness
1 felt weak and exhausted in body, but
my mind wasclear and cheerful, and [ had.
a deep internal conviction that my
oppressor was vanquished, and that [ had
at length regained control of my owr
willand my own bodily organization.

The rays of the sun as it sank to rest,
slanting though rose-colored avenues, fell
upon the gray mists, and crowned the
mountain's summit in arainbowofflory.
The risinlil breeze swept throu%rl) the
forests with a soothing sound, and
eastward the eye was lost in mellow lines of.
golden haze, which to mv soul, freed:
rom captivity, seemed cathedral aisles
of a}oeace. Iroseand descended to the
plain, and was soon on my way
homeward, with a sense of serenity and
happiness to which I hadlong been
astranger, for I knew that the demon that had
possessed me was cast out forever.

Chicago, 11 - Noon. Forty-one persons
were shot in making arrests last night. The
station house was filled with prisoners. The
number of bodies recovered from the ruins
now reaches ninety.
Much suffering has occurred among the
people obliged to camp out on the prairie,
and a number of deaths have resulted. The
relief committee impress all kinds of vehicles
to carry them water and provisions, and are
bringing into churches and school-houses on
the wf st and south sides the immense
quantities of provisions that have arrived, among
them many car loads cooked ready for
distribution. The committee telegraphed to
several places to stop sending more at
present. Twenty car loads of provisions and
10,000 blankets came irom Cincinnati, and
twenty cars from St. Louis. Large
quantities of provisions have arrived from other

cities. All the railroads leading out of
Chicago are carrying the homeless to other
places.
The Common Council have passed an
ordinance fixing tho price of bread at 8 cents for
a loaf of l'.' ounces, and fixing a penalty of
ten dollars for violation of the ordinance."
Cook & Co.'e national hank has resumed
business. All the valuable funds and papers
were seved. *
There is great strife to obtain rooms and
stores for resumption of business.
The relief committee from Cincinnati are
erecti.i g an immense soup house complete in
all its details, and to-morrow will be ready
to distribute 6000 gallons of soup daily.

Shanties are building in the open lots
convenient to the localities and will be made as
comfortable as possible for temporasy
occupancy.
The financial prospect is hourly
brightening. The Republic Insurance Company
expects to pay every dollar of its risks whii h
gives assurance that Chicago companies may
be in better condition than anticipated.

measures for the relief of Chicago. Gov.

FlEST DaV - AfTEBNOOK.
The convention assembled at 2 o'clock.
After some preliminary business, an essay
'•On the Comparative Statistics of Methodism
in Maine," was presented by Rev. 1). B.
Randall. The essayist after a brief intiod
iction, presented several tables illustrating by
figures the various topics contained in the
essay. AVc present a brief synopsis as
follows :
From 1840 to 1850 there was a decrease of
1350, owing to the reaction from the Miller
excitement, the AVcsleyan secession and the
excitement connected with the diversion of
the church in 1844. The Congregationalists

gained during this time 518 and the Baptist
lost 040. From 1850 to I860 the Methodist
gained 3041. From 1800 to 1870 there was a
decrease of 480, occasioned by the war
excitements of 1801-5. The Congregationalists
report in 1870 one minister less than in 1860,
and a gain of 480 members. The Baptist,
during this decade report a decrease of ten
ministers and 2020 members. The F. AV.
Baptists report a decrease of 34 ministers
and 112 members. During the last year the
Methodists gained 13 travelling preachers
and 310 members. The Congregationalists
report during last year a loss of 130
members and the F. VV. Baptist a gain of 12
ministers and 270 members.

Ihe educational interests have also
prospered.
The increase per cent, in the cities and
towns of 5000 inhabitants and upwards, 1850
to 1870, has been viz : - Methodist 5G,
Congregationalist 54, Baptist 39, F. W. Baptist
244; increase in whole State, Methodist 14
1-2, Congregationalist 17 3-4, Baptist 2;
decrease of F. YY'. Baptist G. The loss in rural
places is viz : - Methodist 2,
Congregationalists 31, Baptists 8, F. YV. Baptist 6. By the
same computation the loss in the whele State
is a much less per cent., showing that the
large towns and cities are the strongholds
and gaining places of Methodism.

The church property in Maine, in 1870,
was valued at 8890,985, representing 324
churches and 111 parsonages. There were
285 Sunday schools, 20,603 scholars, 3196
officers and teachers, 57,147 volumes in
libraries; proportion church members to Sabbath
School scholars 119.

The benevolent contributions, including
missionary money in the Maine Conference,
have been, viz 1830, §2490; 1860,
$3597.76; 1870, §7395.59; not embracing home
charities or legacies upon educational
purposes. Increase 1850 to 1860 was 44 1-4 per
cent.; from 1860 to 1870, 1031 percent. In
the East Maine Conference, 1830, §1167;
I860, §1549; 1871, §5469, showing large
increase.
Figures are given to show the meagre
salaries given to ministers compared with other
States, especially the West, and an appeal in
made for a more liberal condition of things,
as the cost of living has proportionately been
larger.

Average salaries in the Maine Conference
.; 1850 was §273; 1860, §394; 1870, §613;
East Maine Conference, 1850, §285; 1860,
Ministers, says Mr. Randall, have some
human nature, and they will not consent to
serve for small pay in Maine, while others,
and in their estimation, equally interesting
fields are open to them at double the salary.
There is no class of men of the same talent
so poorly paid as the ministers of Maine.
The church must absolutely awake to this
matter if she expects to retain her men of
talant.

In conclusion he commends these facts and
figures to the candid consideration of the
convention. "May they teach us humility
and inspire zeal. May the Lord God make
us and all our sister churches a thousand
times as many more as we are, amd bless us
as lie has promised to do.''
At the commencement of this century we
had 7 circuits, 10 ministers, 1197 members -
an increase in five years, 879 members 272
per cent. We have now in 1871, 24,645
members, an increase of 1,959; 219 pastors,
147 local preachers; total 389 ministers.

We number now in the state 4941 more than
the Congregational, 5294 more than the
Baptists of 1870, 9874 more than the Free Will
Baptist. We do not present these facts in an
invideous spirit, but simply to present the
true state of the case. An able essay was
also presented by Rev. E. A. Ilelmcrshausen,
on "Methodism and the State." This was
followed by an interesting description in
which Hon. John J. Ferry, Rev. Stephen
Allen, Rev. Dr. Crook of New York, Rev. A.

Prince, Rev. D. Luce, Campmeeting John
Allen, Rev. Mr. Cushing of Mass., Rev. D.
B. Randall, C. Munger and others. In the
evening we listened to a very able sermon
from Rev. Dr. Crook. 1),

Tbe storm which liegan gently on Tuesday

wind changed to the Northwest about 4 o'clock
and at sunset the air was cool and
auturnnlike. The quantity ot rain which fell duriug

The Presunopscot was said to be quite lull

All the railroads leading out of Portlaud

Trank the road-bed was washed at North
Yarmouth and above Danville Junction so badly
that trains were unable to pass. The 1.10 P.

M. train yesterday ran out aud exchanged
passengers and mails with tbe train from Island
Poud and returned to the city at 5 o'clock.

day after the arrival of the early morning
train from South Paris. The damage wi 1 be
repaired this uiorniug iu season for tbe regular
business. The Portlaud & Kennebec aud
Maine Central Railroads nreseut tbe same

spectacle. So far as we can learn the damage
was greatest east of Watervilie, and the
through trains from Baugor were estopped.
Temporary repairs were at once made to enable
the trails to pass the breaks this morning.
The Portland & Rochester road suffered some
from small breaks, but the trains from
Rochester were not so much delayed as on some of
the other roads. In New Gloucester and
Yarmouth the meadows are overflowed and look
like large ponus, and in some places the

damage comparatively light.

The cost ot travelling in Europe is a
subject that was discussed quite recently by a
fireside circle in this city, and it was thought
that au economical person could spend three
months at an expense of about $oO).
Tinopinion of one who has been there is better
than mere conjecture, and so we give the
statement of Mr. Elweil of the Portland
Transcript. who lias just returned from a
Kuropsan trip:
"As to the cost of travelling in Europe, u
question of great interest to many, it mav be
Staled at about five .dollars gold per day, it
one is economical. It may, of course, cost
much more than that sum. It is perhaps
possible far a gentleman travelling alone, with
little baggage, to do it for less, hut lie must
make up his mind to suffer inconveniences
and practice much self denial, things which

greatly lessen the pleasure of travel. In fact,
to thoroughly enjoy it, one needs plenty of
money. There is a routine ot travel into
which it is easy to get, and out of which it is
difficult to throw one's self, liut one can
see a good deal and enjoy much for five or
six hundred dolliffs, in addition to his passage
money, if he lias the self-denial to refrain
from all unnecessary expenditures."

Yesterday afternoon our citizens had an
opportunity to witness a display supplemental
to the grand military pageant in the streets of
Bangor on the day previous. Five of the
military companies participating in that
celebration, reached this city in a special train at
. quarter to three o'clock in the afternoon, and
made an imposing atreet parade. The com
panies were as follows: Capital Guards, of
Augusta; Portland Light Infantry, of
Portland; Mechanic Blues, of Portland; Auburn
Light Infantry, of Auburn; Norway Light
Infantry, of Norway. They were
accompanied with four bands of music - the Lynn,
Portland, Lewiston and Norway Bands and
two drum corps. On the arrival of the train,
the line formed on Commercial street, the
Capital Guards on the right. Marching down
Bridge and Water streets a halt was made
opposite the post office, where the Capital
Guards saluted the line as it passed by,

and marched to the head of the halted
column, leading the troopers as an escort
through several of the principal streets of the
city. Some preparations had been made for
their coming, and Hags were stretched across
Water street, and depended from stores and

private dwelling* on Water and State street*.
Large crowds lined the sidewalks and filled
the front yard* as tiie soldiers passed by.
It was a display the Like of which ha* not
been seen in our midst since war times.
T ie companies are mostly composed of large,
muscular, noble looking men, many of whom
have seen service in the late war. They did
lot appear fatigued in the least by their long
tourney or active part they had taken in the
'plendid ovations in the "Queen city of the
Mast." After a brief parade the companies
eturned to Market square and marched into
Granite Hall where a collation had been
•pread, and which was partaken of and huge
y relished by the men in arms. At 44 o'clock
he whistle of the locomotive sounded, and
lie companies with the exception of the
Captul Guards were off to Portland, to take part

in llie reception in that city of the President

The Great Bailway Celebration.
Bangor, 19. The exercises of the opening
of the European and North American
Kailway on the part of the Company, took place
to-day at Vanceboro', at half-past eight.
Two trains of cars containing the President
and suite, Governor-General of Canada and
suite, Lieutenant-Governor Wilmotof New
Brunswick, Governor Perliam of Maine, and
suite, and other invited guests to the number
of eight hundred, started from this city and
made the run ty Vanceborough in little less
than five hours. All along the route the
stations were thronged to get a sight of the
President, who gratified them by appearing
un the platform when he was received with
hearty cheers, and waving of handkerchiefs
hy the ladies. The sensation of a train of
Pullman cars with the President of the United

States on board, in the back woods of Maine,
was a novel one to hundreds who saw a
railroad car ether than u eonstructian train for
the first time in their lives one week ago.
The President never seemed happier in
responding to the people than he did to-day
in meeting and greeting the settlers of our
little towns in the wilderness, and many a
young lady will remember with pleasure, and
tell her grand-children with pride, of the kiss
received from the 'Piesident of the United
States, in some of these new settlements,
where one year ago all was a dense forest
Passing the town of Winn the party saw with
surprise, the immense tannery buildings ol
Messrs. Henry Poor & Son, but the surprise
was increased, when on arriving at Kingman,
and seeing the still greater tannery of Shaw

& Kingman, and a village neatly and tastilv
laid out, and were told that but little more
than one year ago all was an unbroken
wilderness.
on arriving at Vanceborough, the place
was found to be gaily decorated in flags oftha
Union of England and of this Dominion,
with a representation of the eagle and lion
on one shield, and the stars and stripes and
St. Georges Cross blended on another.
An immense pavillion had been put up and
tables laid to its entire capacity, with an
elegant and even sumptuous repast and
decorated in a superb 'manner with flags of the
defferent governments represented, and with
boquets, festoons, and garla,.ds of flowers
and evergreens, the question of expense not
having apparently been taken into
consideration.

As the President debarked from the train
a salute was fired, and the Jameson Guards
who had gone up from this city on an earlier
train performed escort dufj-. The train from
St. John arrived at the same time with the
Bangor train, and two peoples were arranged
upon opposite sides of the same tables, where
a general fraternization took place, and
congraulations and compliments were
interchanged. President Jewett of the E. & N. A.
Uailruad, presided, having President Gram
on his right, and Lord Lisgar on his left,
with the other distinguished gentlemen on
each hand. President Jewett called the
assemblage to order, and called upon Prof
Barbour of this city to invoke the divim
blessing, after which the company partook of
the viands before t cm with a keener relish
for the long ride which they had taken.

After the inner man had been satisfied.
President Jewett welcomed the President.
Governor-General, the suites and the
assembled guests, and presented President Grant
amid tumultuous cheers, of which it would be
difficult to sav whether those from Americans
or Provincials were the most hearty.
President Grunt said it was pleasant to hi
here on this occasion, which is celebrated by
the citizens of this continent ot two
nationalities. in which both were equally interest
ed, and sat down amid the cheers' of the
assemblage.

Gov. Wilmot then called for three rousing
cheers for the President, saying that he war
sorry he could not gratily their desire to
visit them at this time, hut shU he would
excuse him if lie would come after his next
election. The cheers were given three times
three.
Lord Lisgar, Governor-General of Canada,
was then introduced, and was received wit!
loud cheers. He said he was extremeh
gratified to be received as the representative
of his Soverign in such an assemblage,
honored as it was by the presence of the
President, which gave it an international char
aeter. lie trusted that tho enterprise over
the completion ot which we to-day rejoice,
would engage the inhabitants of both
countries in amicable interest. He came to-day
expressly to pay a tribute of respect to yuu'i
noble President, not more to the office than

to the man; complimented Iris military
career, and his action in regard to the treaty.
He said the Council of the Dominion would
submit the treaty Ht the next meetingof
Parliament; did not doubt the legislature were in
dined to view the subject from an imperial
and international point of view, and had good
hopes that nothing to mar the good feeling
between the two countries would ever arise.
Stafford North Cole averred to an audience
at Exeter the other day that kindly
disposition toward England existed through this
eonntry to day aince the last shot betweei
tlie countries. Two generations had passed;
1871 was not 1771, and the council ovei
which Gladstone presides are popular eoun
oils, established by the will of tile people.

He hoped the precedents established by the
treaty would stand. Nothing was done by
coercion; the United States was not torn b.
civil service; England was nut threatened
by the fleets of France and Spain, all was
peace. These questions were met not in h
hurtle guise but to reconcile them to peaceful
measures and calm councils. The event will
be recognized in history by the thinking men
in all ages as a greater movement than any
created on battle-fields, &c.
Lieutenant-Governor Wilmot was then
called up. He referred to the exercise* at
Bangor yesterday. They were fit to warm a
man's heart it he had any heart to warm. It
warmed the hearts of all the New
Brunswickera to see the magnificent manner in which
the people had entered upon the ei lcbmtiun ot

Pluck,
©Chicago has been a miracle of
enterprise and growth from the day of its
birth. It is a miracle of pluck and
courage now in the hour of its great
desolation. The Tribune, whose '"fire-prootTM
building, with all its contents, except
oue or two of its power-presses, was
destroyed on Mouday, made its
appearance in a half sheet Wednesday
morning, containing the following brave
editorial:
Cheer up! In the midst of calamity
without parallel in the world's history,
fooking upon the ashes of thirty vears'
accumulation, the people of this once
beautiful city are resolved that Chicago
shall rise again with vigor.

With $200,000,000 or £300,000,000 of
our hard-earned property swept away in
4 tew hours, the hearts of our men and
women are still brave, and they look
in<G the future with undaunted hearts.
<= there has never been such a
calamity, 0 has there never been such
cheerful fortitude in the face of desulation
and ruin.
Already contruets have been made for
rebuilding some of the burned blocks,
and the clearing away of the debris will
begin to-day, if the heat is so far
subdued thst the charred material can be
handled. The money and secarities in
the banks are safe. The railroads are
working with all their energies to bring:
as out of our affliction.

The £300,000,000 of capital invested in
these ruins are bound (o see us through.
They have been built with special
reference t 0 a great commercial Want at this
place, and cannot fail to sustain it.
As Chicago must rise again, we do not
belittle the calamity that has fallen upon
us. The world has probably never seen
the like of it; cetainly not since Moscow
was burned.
Ten or twenty years may be required
to reconstruct our fair city; but capital
will rebuild it, and fire-proof will be
forthcoming. '
The losses we have suffered must be
borne, but the place, time, and men are
here. Commence at the bottom aud
work up again - not at the bottom either,
for we have credit in every land, aud the
experience of one building of Chicago to
help us. g
set us all cheer up, save what is yet

ieft, and we shall come out right. The
Christian world is coming to our relief -
the worst is alveady over. In a few days
more the dangers will be passed, and we
<an resume the battle of life with
Christian faith and Western grit. Let us all
<heer up. / 5

A maultitude of intensely interesting
(incidents of the Chicago fire are related
[b_v those who escaped from the doomed
city. The following are from various
sources:
- The scene in the burnt business
district in the south side is one of terrible
E(lc\':h?lilliull. The whole territory is a
vast swamp of brick, stone, and mortar,
piled in inconceivable heaps of ruin.
'Here and there some building more
sol{idly built than the rest stands erect in
the middle of the vast sea of prostrate
walls around. with its empty windows
and_blackened front telling the story of
Tils destruction. We think the walls of
the Pacific Hotel, the Palmer House, the
Court-House, the Zribune building, and
Field, Leiter & Co.'s dry goods store are
still standing, the buildings having been
icompletely burnt out iuside. Most of
' the buildings burned have fallen in, the

'walls being precipitated inwardly, so
lthat the streets are comparatively free,
and travel about the city not seriously
* incumbered. The roof of the great union
| depot of the Michigan Central road was
l burned off: but the solid stone walls
im'e standing. and it is believed are
un{injured.
| All accounts agree that the heat of the
flames wasintense beyond all conception.
Unbroken walis of stone or brick or iron,
with roofs of the same material, would
crumble away like sand before it.

| The Tribune pressmen kept their
presses running, working off the outside
of the paper, while the rirc raged all
around them. At length, at the latest
moment for escape, they became aware
that the building was not fire-proof.

At the Tremont House the elevator
became useless, and the sleeping guests, a
[ large numberbeing babies, hurried down
[ stairs. The clatter of the removal of
tranks and the hurrying of domestics
[impeded the passagewavs. Several
per| sons in their eagerness jamped down the
| staivs and;limped away. Others, in their
| haste, left beneath their pillows watches
[and money, only discovering their losses
{when they had reached the Michigan
{ Central Depot - then supposed to be a
| perfectly safe place. A crowd of persons
| hastened thither, some carrying beds,
| some sewing-machines, and one lady had
{ six canary birds in a cage, in one hand,
{and an immense family Bible in the
{other. Shesaid: 'I was determined to
| bring these off, if I lost all the rest."
!Auothm' young woman was seen
carryling two large paintings, evidently those

{of her father and mother. She was but
| partially clad, and amongst all her
house| hold wealth songhtto preserve these filial
{ mementoes as being toher most precious.
{ A Mr. Farrar reports the scenes in
| Chicago during Mouday and Monday
(night as appalling in the extreme. Many
! persons became crazed and jumped into
' the river, whileseveral stabbed aud killed
| themselves in their desperation. Those
|in the immediate neighborhood of the
| fire attempted to save their property,
| loading it on wagons. The horses,
be]comiug wild and unmanageable, rushed
through the strects, knocking down
men, women and children,and dashedon
into the flames, and were destroyed.

Children where left to care for
themselves, and sat on the curbstones, waiting
for their fathers and mothers. The fire
would seem to cease for a few moments,
thenrush on withredoubled
vigor,sweeping every thing before it, eating its way
into the Nicholson pavement, which was
one sheet of flame for miles.
As early as Monday afternoon
tradesmen began to be crazed by the thoughts
of what they must lose; they lost
common_ sense, and put pillage into the
minds of the people. Groecers and
clothiers opened their shop doors and let
whoever chose take what he would. A
jeweler in Lake street so tar forgot his
duty as a good citizen, when the public
was threatened with danger, that he
actually opened his store, ran into the
street, and begg«d passers-by to help
bhim save his treasures; and of course

they were not loth to accede to his
re| quest, and openly pocketed watches,
'necklaces, and diamonds, and coolly
walked away. The good jeweler
him| self had, like a foolish citizen, contrived
| to make lawlessness take on the
appeariance of law. Such scenes as these
occurring throughout the city, made a mob
of the people, ordinarily law-abiding
enough. They could not save their own
property,vetthey might reimburse
themselves for their lossesby taking the
abandoned property of others as it came in
their way; and from abandoned goods
to those merely separated by lock, and
key and door, the step was easy.

Seeing the cashier of one of the banks
rush into his office as the flames were
bearing almost upon the building, a
thief watched his exit. It was not long
before the official appeared with his
dtms fall of money packages and bonds,
and no sooner had he appeared than the
thief prostrated him with a blow upon
the side of the head, and grabbed a
portion of the treasure. A policeman in an
instant saw what was done and grabbed
the villain, who drew a pistol and shot
the faithful officer through the heart,
and. then sprang through the excited
crowd, brandishing his pistol and
endeavoring to make good his escape. But
the sight, with all the surrounding
circumstances, had maddened the
bystanders to frenzy, and they fell upon the
wretch like so many tigers, tearing him
from limb to limb to limb, and literally

disemboweling him.
A Mr. Stevens, returning home from
his burning store with a safi heart, says
the spectacle that presented itself to him
in many of the side streets was one that
he shall never forget. The smoke was
dense, and he had to place a
handkerchief over his mouth to escape
smothering. He saw, he thinks, not less than
twenty men, women, and children expire
around him from exhaustion, and some
'were stifled. In looking behind as he
was hurrying away, he saw the flames
'gaining.on him, and above the uproar of
all he could sometimes hear the piercing
scream of some unfortunate being.

Another merchant, describing his
narrow escane from the flames, relates the
following: Just now occurred a scene
that froze our blood. At the
intersection of Randolph and Market streets was
a large building (Callom's) used for
offices. The ganitor resided on the fourth
floor with his family, consisting of a
wife and four children. By some means,
they were unable to escape.
Surrounded gy the fire, they ascended to the roof.
The babe was in thc mother's arms, and
another child, a little boy, clung to her
skirts, Two girls were clasged in the
arms of the father. Their shouts were
but faintly heard over the howl of
the winds and the roar of the flames.

At last the heat became so intense
that the woman was overcome and
fell to the roof. Thefather wildlg' threw
out his hand and sufixered, writhed and
sank by his wife's side. That was all of

that tragedy. We sickened at the sight,
aud hurried down t 0 the street, which
by this time was pretty well deserted.
Then along the banks of the lake we
wandered, mere like dead than living
men. We heard and saw mourning and
agony and suffering that all the books in
the world could not hold the account of.
We were comfortably fixed in life one
week ago; and now we are penniless.
The lady school-teacher, heretofore
mentioned, tells some strange
experiences: * One incident combined the
pathetic with the ridiculous. "T'wo blocks
beyond where I lived in Halstead street
resided an old German, an almost
helpless cripple, whose sole support was his
wife and young son. The latter went
away in the morning and did net return.

The five rapidly approached with deadly |
omen, and the old couple were not only
distracted at the absence of the boy, but
fearful of their possible fate. At last the
flames came so near that they must fly
or die. In the strength of her affection,
the old woman seized the poor eripple,
placed him upon her back, and thus stag- |
gered along the distance of two blocks, |
when some men placed him in a grocer's |
wagon and drew him to a place of
safety. One of the little girls that attended '
my school became lost. I found her
crying as though her heart would break.

She is but seven years old, and she could
not tell what had become of her parents
and family. There were many such
cases. As we went onfarther, the throng
increased until the streets and sidewalks
were black with people. It was like a
freshet, and poured in the one direction
of safety. By and by we found the fire
getting avound us, as though escape
would be cut off and we wouid be
entomed in one grand pyre of flame. 'Go
the other way; we are headed off!' was
now and then thecry, and the multitude
would turn back, struggling in a new
direction. I saw some women and
children and one man, exhausted, lie down
in the gutters to diein the hopelessness
of desperation. Others would seize and
urge them along. Smoke and cinders
and flame and scorching heat filled the

air. Children screamed in terror and
begged for water. Some would catch
up water from puddles near hydrants
and moisten the mouth. 'This is
hellfire!" 'Thisis the day of judgment!'
'This must be the end of the world!'
were the exclamations heard. The
degree of sympathy that prevailed was
wonderfal. There seemed to be one
instinctive throb »f feeling, and the strong
helped the weak.
The following additional bodies have
'been identified: Henry J. Ullman, firm
of Wren, Ullman & Co., burned; Patrick
Foley, shot; Edward Honey, burned.

It is Tumored that Ullman was murdered
'instead of suffocatcd. His body was
found near his banking-house, which he
'had evidently just left with money and
valuables in his arms.
During Tuesday and Wednesday night
intense excitement reigned in the
southern district. A large number of shots
were fired. A negro who was
discovered setting fire to a house was killed.
Nearly all the destroyed business
premises have placards posted on stakes,
designating the new locations
establish'ed by the proprietors.
~ Out of forty corpses discovered in one
place, all but two were without a
vestige of clothing, with the exception of
an occasional boot. The sights
piesented were sickening beyond description.

Strong men who had saved their lives,
in vain attempted to save others.
Women who were able to escape, but who
would not leave their offspring and frail
children, went down in the buildings
and perished in their helplessness. Two
familics on the north side, near the lake,
procured wagons, and, placing the
wo' men and chi(fren in them, drove to the
lake shore, where they were obliged to
remain through one whole day and night,
driving into the water at intervals to
'keep from being consumed. They were
finally rescned by a tug-boat, nearly all
of them in an exhausted condition. It
is thought the weaker ones can not
recover.

| - There was an insurance of $225,000 on
l the Chamber of Commerce building, of
' which probably SIOO,OOO will be
obtain|ed from the company. The structure is
J to be rebuilt on the old site immediately.
. The general feeling in the community
is growing more cheerful. It is as
surprising as encouraging, to see so many
evidences of faith and courage among
those who were at first supposed to be
hopelessly crushed and ruined. Many
have enough means left to resume
business; while others, backed by offers of
help from wealthy friends in other parts
of the country, are also arranging for
'rebuilding and resuming.

~ The contributions of money, food,and
materials are literally overwhelming, but
will all be needed and thankfully
received. A sentiment of gratitude
pervades the whole community for the
unexampled exhibition of generosity
displayed by the people of the whole
country. |
The dawn of each succeeding day
brings brighter prospects, and the hope
of the energetic men who made Chicago
what it was is strengthened.
Twentyone columns of the Zribune this
morning were filled with advertisements of |
business changes. Builders are
overwhelmed with applications to put upnew
houses. One man made sixteen contracts
last night. Little is doing in produce
circles, but commission merchants and
grain dealers are hard at work preparing
to open on their usnal scale by next
week. The agency of the Atna
Insurance Company are paying their losses,
which they claim will not reach $3,000,-

000. The county supervisors to-day
resolved to rebuild the court-house at
once. The amount of funds saved from
the vaults of the banks, added to the
balances in New York, leaves them with an
amount of cash equal to about 40 or 50
per cent. This, with the insurance that
will be paid, insures the collection of 75
per cent. of their loans by the banks.
The Liverpool, London and Globe
Insurance Company has ordered the payment
of its losses immediately. 'Che
aggregate loss of this company is about two
millions, The loss of the Commerce of
Albany is $450,000. This company has
been placed in the hands of receivers,
Mayor Mason has issued a
'Froclamation in which he says: ¢ Order reigns
supreme, and life and property are as
secure as before the buruinf of the city.

The city government in all its
departments is now in full and complete
operation. None of our inhabitants are
without shelter of some kind. Food to relieve
present necessities has flowed in upon
us in abundance from all quarters, but a
long winter is before us, and we shall
ineed all the aid sgmpatlxizing humanity
can render. Such an exhibition of
sympathy and generous aid as was called
forth by our great calamity never before
'was equaled in the history of the world.
It has cheered and enconrn%ad our
citizens. Business largely has been resum-

ed. Houses, mostly of a temporary
character, are springing up in all parts of the
2000 acres of ruins. Many permanent
buildings are being erected, and the
energy of ourcitizens is being everywhere
displayed. In the name of our citizens, I
tender heartfelt thanks to all who so
nobly and generously have sympathized
with and aided us in our great distress."

ARGUMENT OF THE COUNSEL
A BRIEF HISTORY OF THE CASE
The argument in the case of Mr. John
Fazcnde, charged with the murder of Marie
Estelle, a mulatto girl, commenced to-day
in the parish court of Jefferson, before Judge
Kern. District Attorney McKay, on the
part of the State, quoted from several legal
authorities to show that the beating the
girl received by Fazende was the remote
cause of death and consequently held that
the accused was guilty of murder. J. J.
Roman, on the part of the defense, followed
with an able argument; most of his efforts,
however, were devoted to comparing the
testimony of witnesses of the State to show
discrepancies. Judge Scott followed, and
at 3 P. M., the court adjourned to 10 A. M.,
October 13,1871, when R. King Cutler will
speak, and the district attorney will then
close the argument on the part of the State.

BRIEF HISTORY OF THE CASE.
Marie Estelle, a beautiful mulatto girl of
about eighteen years, had been a servant
girl in the the employ of John Fazende.
The girl Marie, among her ether duties,
had the coffee to make in the morning,
w hich was usually made by the use of a
spirit lamp, On the morning of August 27,
1871, she lit the lamp and again retired.
The lamp exploded, and the flames ignited
and run on the floor. Fazende called the
girl, Marie, and took her by the arm and
brought her to see what he said she had
done. He then told her she must leave,
and took her to the door to put her out.

At this point the testimony differs in the
following particulars: The State claim,
supported by several witnesses, that as
they got on the gallery, Fazende
struck her and she fell down,
where he jumped'on her with his knees on
her breast. On the part of the defense,
supported by witnesses, that at the door
they fell down. Madame Fazende falling
with them. However, after this the girl
went home sick, and in eight days after
died. A post-mortem examination was
held, and resulted in the arrest of Mr.

Fazende on the charge referred to. The
girl Marie was more of an associate of the
female portion of the family than a servant,
having been with them more than five
years, sleeping with them, going to church,
$tc.
The case has attracted considerable in
terest, owing to the high social position of
Mr. Fazende. His family, composed of
several beautiful and highly accomplished
young ladies, have been in constant at
tendance.

Foreign Commerce of Boston.
The Boston Transcript says:
The foreign trade of this port -thus far
this season shows a marked improvement
over last year. To-day a fleet of vessels
came into port laden with rich and valuable
cargoes, among which were two ships from
the East Indies, two ships and one brig from
Europe, and several from the West Indies.
The aggregate value of the goods on board
these vessels will amount to a very large
sum. There is also a large fleet from foreign
countries on the way to this port, many of
which are now due. They number in all
nearly a hundred sail of vessels, among
which are twenty-two from the East Indies,
and forty-nine from different ports in
Europe.

The total value of foreign imports at the
port of Boston during the past nine months
amounts to about £50.000,600, which is a
gain of upward of $10,000,000 over the
same period last year.

We propose to wait for the returns
before announcing the result of the election in
Texas. The Houston Union of the tenth
instant contains the following distinct and
separate editorial paragraphs:
At every poll that the Democracy have
placed two boxes for the deposition of
tickets the votes will be declared
invalidated. They did this for intimidation, and
the tickets will be thrown out.
Our victory in this State will draw to the
Republican standard hundreds of old
confederate soldiers, who have been kept back
from fear that the peijured Democracy
would get into power and ostracise them.

Considering the completeness of their
defeat. the Democracy keep their lip up pretty
well, still their chagrin crops out
nevertheless; like the boy who "saw" the fourth of
July, and who discovered his mother the
day after observing his bachanalian antics,
sought to disguise his tipsiness by
exclaiming, "I'm not drunk, mother; but a sicker
child tou never had."
The emigration to Texas will increase
five-told this fall because of the election of
the Republican candidates. The most of
this emigration will come from' Georgia,
Alabama and Mississippi, and they are
attracted here by the wonderful growth of
Texas under the Republican administration
They prefer to leave their old homes be
cause many of them have been destroyed,
anil many of their neighbors have passed
away during tile war, and they are
solicitous to emigrate where they can have
advantages which they do not possess at their

old homes.
The Democrats claimed the State and the
election of all their candidates, immediately
aiter the last day's voting, and before the
votes were counted. They have done the
same thing in regard to Louisiana when
this State had gone strongly Republican, as
the counting of the votes has shown subse
quently.

The Chicago Grate Trade.
Now is the golden opportunity for New
Orleans to secure the Chicago grain trade.
The capacity of the grain elevators there,
most or all of which were destroyed by the
recent tire, was 11.580,000 bushels. Chicago
can not now store grain there, and hence
the important question was asked by Mr.
John Newell, of Chicago, in a dispatch to
Colonel James T. Tucker, general Southern
agent of the Illinois Central railroad in this
city:
Can yon open shipments of produce, via
New Orleans, coastwise and abroad ?

Grain, if it can be transhipped here, can
be poured down to Cairo over the Illinois
Central railroad, and thence brought to
New Orleans in bulk hy barges. We
repeat, now is the golden opportunity to
secure the grain and produce trade of
Chicago and the West.

Chicago and Charity.
The terrible loss of life and property by
the late fire in Chicago has elicited the
sympathies of .America and Europe in behalf
of the suffering families of that unfortunate
city, and millions of dollars are coming
from both countries to their relief.
We are glad that the citizens of Chicago
cannot complain of
" the rarity
Of human charity
Under the sun ; "
and we earnestly hope that the millions of
money yet needed to repair their pecuniary
losses may be speedily supplied. In this
case what is done should be done quickly.

While we of the South are wearing summer
clothing, and inhaling the odor of autumnal
roses, thousands of men, women, and
children, in Chicago, homeless, houseless,
and comparatively naked, are shivering in
the winds and frosts of an unusually early
northern winter, and are literally sitting
in dust and ashes.
We deeply regret in this connection to
notice among some of our people, and we
are glad to know the number is very small
a disposition to look at this matter in an
improper light. While they are perfectly
willing to subscribe, and do subscribe
liberally, for the relief of Chicago, they arc
fond of alluding to the fact that but a few
years ago Chicago subscribed liberally to
the equipment and maintenance of soldiers
who burned our towns and villages, and
ttirned our women and children into the
public street. They profess to rccognise

in the Chicago calamity a just visitation
of God, and a striking illustration of the
saying that "Cur.ses like chickens come
home to roost" They seem to say. to the
Chicago sufferers, "You deserve no
sympathy from us ; you laughed at our
calamity ; and we rejoice in the opportunity of
returning good for evil. We are oppressed
by tyranny, and impoverished by taxation,
and we owe it to you and to your kind ;
but out of our limited means we give you
charity, and we do it to show you that we
are magnanimous."
Now we humbly submit that this is all
wrong. Whether God has or has not
scourged Chicago for her moral or her
political sins, is none of our business. If we
have a fine chance to pour coals of fire upon
her already scorched and blackened head,

by giving her food and drink, we should be
far from rejoicing that we have the chance.
No one should rejoice at human suffering,
and no one should return good for evil
merely to proclaim his magnanimity. There
is no real charity in such a feeling, and
though with it our money may flow like
water, it will place nothing to our credit
when the books are opened in the great day
of accounts. Charity is not puffed up. True
benevolence seeks no counsel from selfish
pride. When women are houseless, and
children are starving and freezing, it is no
time to talk about the sins of their husbands
and fathers, nor to accompany charity with
reproaches, and lectures on merit. The
great and imperative dut}' is to give, and to
give freely and kindly. " God loveth a
cheerful giver." ~

We will publish next week an article
from an exchange, detailing briefly the
horrors of the Chicago conflagration. It will be
seen that the demons of murder, arson and
robbery, assisted the devouring flames in
their fearful work of destruction. The
necessity for relief is urgent, and will not admit
of delay. For the sake of common humanity
let us come up to the rescue. For the honor
of our proverbially generous people we hope
to see public meetings called all over the
South for the purpose of relieving the
Chicago sufferers throughout the coming
winterDistrict Court.

The Eighth District Court, Judge John
E. King, presiding, opened at Opelousas
last Monday. But little business has been
done this week, except by the Grand Jury.
The most important business-that will
come before the Court, is that of a
criminal nature. Crime cannot be checked
exccpt by punishment; and that
punishment, to be effective, must result from
the action of judicial tribunals. It is a
matter of notoriety that many murders
have been comitted here, and that few,
comparatively none of the murderers have
been tried and punished. Few are indicted,
fewer tried, andstMl fewer convicted.
Wit* *
nesses are afraid to testify, and avoid
testifying, because, they have lost all faith in the
certainty of punishment following proof; it
is not safe to have a murdoeer for a
neighbor against whom you have testified in
court. Heinous crimes are continually
committed, and it is almost impossible to find

out the perpetrators, on account of this
feeling and fear on the part of witnesses. It is
indeed a deplorable state of affairs, and it
cannot be easily changed except by the
action of the judiciary. Murders are
committed because the murderers have no fear of
punishment; witnesses will not testify
against them because they fear them more
than they respect the law which is seldom
enforced. A murderer tried shortly after
the commission of the crime, when the proof
is plain and easily obtained, and public
feeling against him, may be convicted ; but by
appeals, new trials, and the many other
delays known tÔ legal practice, the final
disposition of the case is postponed, until
public feeling has died out, and witnesses
disappeared, when acquittal, or punishment
merely nominal compared with the enormity
of the offence, follows as a matter of course.

Any one who will revie*f, in his own recol.
lection, the homicides that have been
committed, the trials for homicide, and how
many have been punished for the same, will
admit that these remarks are correct. The
feeling is general, among all classes of
people, that no one, especially one who can
command money, and has influential friends,
will be punished for homicide. We have
heard this feeling expressed often, at all
times and places, and by all classes. *
It rests with the Grand Jury, the Petit
Jury, the Sheriff, the District Attorney and
the District Judge, to rid the community of
this great and growing evil ; and especially
do the industrious, peaceable and
law-abiding citizens look to them for vigorous
measures against the law-breakers, at the
present term of the District Court.

Gen. Hade Hampton's Advice.
Gen. Hampton, of South Carolina, advises
the Southern Democracy to take no part in
the next National Democratic Convention,
and gives (lie following reasons for so doing :
"1. The Southern delegates in a national
convention could exercise no influence in
shaping the policy, making up the issues,
or selecting the candidates for the next
contest, without seriously injuring the prospect
j of a Democratic triumph. That this would
inevitably be the case is proven by the
result of the last Democratic Convention,
where the very presence of Southerners was
used to prejudice the action and to defeat
the candidate of our party.

" 2., If the Southern candidates could not
with propriety exert any influence in the
Convention, while their mere altendance in
it might result in infinite mischief to the
Democratic party, it is surely the part of
wisdom to refrain from participating in the
deliberations of the convention.
" 3. The Northern Democracy will have
to bear the burden of the fight in the next
Presidential contest, and it is only right that
they should choose the field and select the
standard-bearers."

National Colored Convention.
Charleston, Oct. 22. - The National
Colored Convention met in Columbia on
Wednesday. Lieutenant Governor Ransier, of
South Carolina, being permanent president.
On Thursday resolutions endorsing
President Grant's administration were introduced
and referred. Resolutions were adopted
advocating the preservation of the
reconstructed State Governments and existing
laws, and the continuance in power of the
Republican party, alsn endorsing those
Republicans who have come to the South from
the North, and deprecating an'attack npon
class within the Republican ranks.
Resolutions were introduced on Friday
deprecating emigration to Liberia.

Congressman Elliott, of South Carolina,
submitted yesterday an address to the
American people. It asks for a more perfect
recognition of the colored people in the
workshops and all other industrial pursuits,
that they may become proficient in
mechanical sciences, and thereby protect skilled
artisans from having to compete in the
market with workmen of inferior capacity. It
asks from Congress aid for the education of
the poor children of the South. It demands
one standard of duty or policy for all
citizens, and no especial favor but to deal with
all alike. It affirms that the colored
citizens have no desire to strike a line of action
not common to the whole people, and
concludes with a hope for a speedy abolition of
slavery in every part of the world.
