~ An Account of Terrible Suffering.
~ On the 15th there arrived in New
York city by the Erie railway a number
of persons direct from the scenes of the
great, forest fires in Wisconsin and
Michigan. There were nine in the
party: James W. Hunter, Mrs. Sarah
Hanter, George Martine, of Flushing,
L. 1., Henry Porter, Samuel Hillman,
Charles Myers of Freehold, N. J.,
Margaret MeGorm, Edward Wallace and
George Blakeslee of New York. All
were suffering from having inhaled the
smoke, fumes and ashes of the fire.

Mrs. Hunter's hair, which she says
flowed to the waist, was completely
burned off. One side of her face "and
neck and shoulders were fearfally
injured, three deep holes baving been
made by the glowing cinders in the
flesh. Her hands, also, were covered
with blisters. Mr. Hunter's face, neck
and hands were badly burned. Mr,
Martine's face was a hideous spectacle.
One' cheek was literally raw, and great
blotches pitted his left arm, shoulder
and back. One eye is hopelessly ruined,
and the other inflamed to an ominous
degree. All were scarred, especially
on the face, neck, hands and feet. As
they all say, no tongue can tell their
agony of mind, pain, anguish and
terror, nor can language or pencil portray
the dreadful scenes through which they
have passed.

Mr, Hanter says he resided at
Prestigo with his wife and little child, seven
years of age. Their house was about
three miles from the town, just at the
edge of a strip of forest. There had
been fires in the woods and prairies for
a week previous, and night after night
they had sat at the windows, gazing
upon the gorgeous panorama of flame,
smoke and sparkling cinders, as it
moved along the horizon. Very little,
it any, fear was entertained, as the
course of the fire seemed away from the
town. |

On Sunday night they attended church
in the village. They and Martin, the
herdman, retired to rest early, wholly
unsuspecting the fearful peril that was
soon to overwhelm them. At about
midnight they were aroused by the
roaring and crackling of the flames. At
first they were almost petrified with
amazement and fear. The blazing
wood seemed marching upon them. A
brisk breeze was stirring, but the strong
current of hot air raged to and fro with
|2 horrid, howling sound. Quickly
|dressiug, they rushed to theyard. The
lsky was thick with smoke, and showers
of sparks were hurled hither and thither,
lassailing their faces, eyes and clothing.

lFrom the barn came a piteous chorus
of neighs, bellowings and screams from
the terrified cattle, horses and other
animals. After great difficulty they were
released, and compelled to goout. The
cattle atoncestampeded from the fire, but
the horses trembled and scemed
paraiyzed, their nostrils extending, their
eyes dilating and glaring and their
mouths frothing. With great difficulty
and haste they were harnessed and
attached to a long lumber box wagon,
into which a few articles were thrown,
and the party mounted and drove off.

An eighth of a mile had been traversed
at a rapid rate, when a sudden gust of
wind drove a mass of red hot cinders
upon them, filling the air with stiffing
smoke. Where the sparks fell they
burned into the flesh. The little girl
screamed with fear. 'Oh, mamma, I
am burning up," she cried; the others
shook off the fire and covered
themselves with blankets. The air for a
moment was black, and breathing was
almost impossible. The horses
staggered, backed, and reared with furious
screams, and then with a plunge that
unseated those in the wagon, rushed
down the road at almost lightning
speed. All control of them was lost,
and the party clung to thé sides of the
vehicle to keep in. On they flew, the
wheels striking fire against the stones,
and the wagon swaying toand fro frc..

one side of the road to the other. Then,
for a time, the wind changed and the
clouds of cinders were carried in
another direction. They could see that all
the northern part of the village was on
fire, and the flames seemed moving
with the velocity of clouds. All the
baildings were of wood, mueh of it
being of pitch pine, and as there bad been
no rain for a long time, and the san had
baked everything dry, the fire ran along

thedr'as though they had been a train
of gunpowder. '
Mrs. Hunter said: We stood in tbe'
water up to our necks, our little girl
Mionie being held up between us.!
When we first went in the feeling was
that of grateful refreshment. The top
of the water seemed warm, but the
bottom part was cold. After we had been
there half an hour, the wind carried
great strips, and even pieces of board,
some of them flaming. These would
be whirled in the air, high up over our
heads, and and hover like a huge hawk,
and then swoop down upon us. We
would duck our heads under the water,
but would get so exhausted that we
could net,and then we had to be burned.

Poor little Minnie, so weak that she
could bardly ery, would say: ¢Dear
papa, I am burned again; dear
mamma, my feet are so cold, and I am so
tired. Three hours and more thus
passed. Every moment we expected
todie. Finally the air became so thick
that we coulinot see® Oureyesseemed
parboiled. The agony was awful. Our
feet were like ice, and our faces and
headsin an atmosphere of flame. Atlast
there was a rush of the waters, the dam
had given away, and the flood came
dowun upon us, sweeping us off our feet
into a mass oftimber and broken planks,
some on fire, horses, cattle, dogs and
human Dbeings all struggling and
shrieking. In the rush and whirl the
almost helpless Mr. and Mrs. Hunter
were separated, Mrs. Hunter went
down and came near being drowned.

Minnie was lost and drowned. By a
swerving of the current they were
washed on shore, and at daylight found
each other. There were many
mourning and erying over the scene of
desolation. On all sides, as far as the eye
could reach, there were smouldering
fires. The village was a long waste of
ashes; not a vestige remained.

in a prosecution for selling rum, the
jury returned a verdict of ''not guilty"
when the evidence of guilt was most
conclusive. Judge Barrows, who
